name: crandel
author: clothes-dressing-packing designer
description: Washing hanging on lines. CLUE `gaps/longs/drips`, e.g. `524/43/11`: `gaps` = one digit per LINE (3 or 4 lines, each 2-6, total 6-11) = how many rows of air hang under that line; `longs` and `drips` = one digit each per line EXCEPT the last. SOLUTION: an ASCII drying rack, all rows the same width (the drawer picks 26-32). A row whose characters are only '=' and 'v' is a LINE ('v' = a peg, cosmetic and unchecked); every other row is air. A GARMENT is a horizontal run of one capital letter; it hangs from the line above, i.e. it must appear in the top row of its block and the identical run must repeat down to its hem, so garments are rectangles and the set of runs in each row must be a subset of the row above. Anything else (filler char, letters, widths, hems, pegs, how many garments) is free. THE TWO PINNED NUMBERS, per line except the last: (1) `longs[i]` = how many garments on line i hang ALL THE WAY DOWN to the line below (hem in the last row of the gap); (2) `drips[i]` = how many of THOSE have at least one garment hanging directly underneath them from the next line (their columns overlap) - "how many of the ones that reach are dripping on the washing below". drips[i] < longs[i] always, so every line always shows at least one long garment hanging over a bare stretch. PRIVATE - INTENDED DISCOVERY PATH: one demo gives "washing on lines"; the grammar is rebuilt in 1-2 demos; field 2 ("how many hang right down") is the foothold and is guessable from one demo; field 3 is the lateral step, and the two rivals one step away - counting all the long ones (that is field 2, so it is visibly not field 3) and counting the garments that merely have something under them - are both false on EVERY line of EVERY shipped demo, because solve() rejects any picture in which any of 14 rival per-line readouts equals the drips vector: pairs (a long garment over two counts twice), wet (the garments below that are being dripped on), cover (fully covering instead of overlapping), garments per line, short garments, short-with-something-below, wide garments, long-and-wide, long-and-narrow, long-not-at-either-end, long-over-two. WITNESS TABLE (500 fresh clues; every attacker knows the grammar AND field 2 and differs only in the law it uses for field 3): true rule 100%; "fully covers something below" 25.5%; "long and over two" 16.2%; "not at the end of the line" 16.8%; "wide" 15.2%; "in the left half" 13.6%; random choice of which long ones 12.6%; "narrow" 9.4%. TEMPLATES: identical garment columns on every line, so every long garment automatically has something under it (this scored 87% against an earlier one-digit version) 0.0%; two garments a line 0.0%; previous answer replayed 0.0%; one fixed answer for all clues 0.8%; empty/junk/clue echoed 0.0% (20000 junk strings: no raise, no non-binary, worst 0.15 ms). ~9800 distinct clue classes, so brute-force-and-cache over 6x450 probes is worth ~12% of the final on top of the 12.6% blind rate. HYPOTHESIS ELIMINATION: over a family of 150 per-line readouts (any/long/short x below/nothing-below/two-below/covers/covered x wide/narrow x inner-only, plus pair and lower-line counts), 6.6 survive one demo, 1.6 survive two and the true rule is the ONLY survivor after 3-6 demos in 30/30 trials - the demos are informative, the search is the difficulty. Author: clothes/dressing/packing direction.
